question: An analyst has condensed a twenty-page Claude-produced analysis into a one-page version for an executive committee that will act on it directly. Which check matters most before she circulates the shorter version?
options: A) That the one-page version reads in the same house style as the committee papers her team has circulated in previous quarters.
B) That the one-page version comes in under the length the committee asked for, since executive committee papers are capped at a single side.
C) That the one-page version is worded differently enough from the long analysis for the two documents to be told apart easily.
D) That nothing removed in the condensing changes the recommendation, particularly any condition on which that recommendation depends.
correct_answers: D) That nothing removed in the condensing changes the recommendation, particularly any condition on which that recommendation depends.
explanations: House style helps a paper land well with a familiar audience, but it is a presentation concern. A perfectly styled summary can still have lost the qualification that made the recommendation safe.
Meeting the length limit is a formatting requirement that must be satisfied anyway, and it is easy to check. It says nothing about whether the shortened paper still supports the decision being made.

Distinguishing the two documents is a filing convenience at best. Deliberately rewording for difference risks introducing changes of meaning rather than protecting the committee from acting on a distorted summary.

Correct. Adapting for an audience must not change what the audience will do. A caveat or condition dropped in the interests of brevity turns a qualified recommendation into an unqualified one for the people acting on it.
